submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole fires on the constituent that follows a copula or auxiliary in a clause where the element the verb governs has been displaced to that slot: the associate NP after existential 'there is/are/was/were' (peaking on the quantifier/determiner that opens it and on its head noun — no, some, more, much, many, any), the postponed subject of a root wh-/yes-no question ('Is the president correct?', 'What is cloud computing?'), and the last word or closing comma of an adverbial inserted between an auxiliary and its complement ('were, in the end, published'). The same words stay near zero when nothing is displaced: NPs in pre-verbal subject position ('Much doubt about the plan remains'), a plain article+noun complement of a non-existential copula ('It is a question of time'), and ordinary declaratives ('The results were published').

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The modern passport is a surprisingly recent invention. For most of the nineteenth century, travellers crossing the borders of Europe carried letters of introduction, letters of credit, and, if they were fortunate, a document signed by a consul who happened to know their family. The notion that a state should issue a standard booklet to every citizen, and that every citizen should be obliged to carry it, would have struck most people as an unnecessary intrusion. Railways changed the argument. Once a worker could travel six hundred miles in a single day, the old assumption that strangers were rare and recognisable collapsed, and governments began to look for a cheap way to sort the honest traveller from the fugitive. The first experiments were clumsy. Some countries printed a single page, folded it twice, and stamped it with a wax seal that broke whenever the paper was opened. Others required the traveller to obtain a fresh signature at every frontier, which meant that a journey from Paris to Vienna might consume a dozen sheets and as many afternoons. Consular clerks complained about the workload, railway companies complained about the delays, and no one was satisfied except the stationers, who sold the forms at a handsome profit. Reform came slowly, and usually after a scandal. In 1914 a German clerk in a small border town refused to accept a British family's papers because the photograph had been taken eleven years earlier; the family missed their ship, the story reached the newspapers, and within a year the standard booklet with a recent photograph was being printed in three colours. The war accelerated everything. Every state suddenly wanted to know who was inside its territory, and the booklet became a tool of security as much as a convenience. By the 1920s the format was broadly settled: a cover, a photograph, a description of the bearer, and a page for visas. There were many practical objections to the new system, most of them raised by shipping companies who feared that the paperwork would discourage casual travel. Their lobbyists argued that a family of modest means would rather stay at home than queue for photographs, and that the tourist trade would wither. The objections were answered, in the end, by the economics of the shipping lines themselves: a passenger with papers was easier to insure, and the first-class trade grew rather than shrank. The League of Nations convened a conference in 1920, and although the delegates disagreed about almost everything else, they agreed on the size of the booklet, the colour of the cover, and the number of pages. The agreement was not binding, but it was convenient, and convenience is usually enough. The postwar boom tested the system again. Air travel made the frontier meaningless for a while, and by the 1960s a businessman might cross four borders in a single morning. Yet the booklet survived, partly because airlines found it a convenient identity check, and partly because states were reluctant to give up a document that told them, at a glance, who was arriving. The photograph became the most important page. Forgery grew more sophisticated, and so did the printing: watermarks, holograms, and machine-readable strips. None of this changed the basic idea, which is that a traveller should be able to prove who he is without the help of a consul.
